title: [D4 Policy] Deterministic escalation evaluator independent of triage
summary: `helena.policy.v1.escalate` is `concept/04`'s second, independent input to the analyst: it reads every claim the context holds (`helena.policy.supports_in`), applies the tier test, the per-source confidence threshold loaded from `config/policy.toml`, and the same composition-rule predicates task 32 froze, and returns an `Escalation` naming the evidence ids that caused it and every candidate that did not, with the rules that held each one back. It takes no `AgentResult`, no `AgentFailure` and no `Decision` — there is no parameter a verdict could arrive through — so a triage `normal` and a triage typed failure are both computed past rather than around.
assumption_validated: That `concept/04`'s escalation sentence decomposes into three deterministic tests over what the store already holds, and that the third of them can reuse the composition rule rather than restate it. It does: the tier is `ESCALATING_TIERS`, the classification is the claim's own evidence-level root, and 'whose traffic characteristics support it' is `_contacted_with_traffic_both_ways`, `_is_shared_infrastructure` and `port_matched` — the identical helpers `constrain` reads, so one `policy_version` cannot hold two opinions about one claim. Five mutations were checked and each failed the suite: `<` to `<=` on the threshold, dropping the tier gate, counting rows instead of `source_diversity`, dropping the domain rule, and dropping the freshness gap. TWO NEGATIVE RESULTS, both recorded as passing tests rather than prose. (1) DOMAIN HITS DO NOT ESCALATE AT ALL. The scope test works on address entities and not on domain ones, and `concept/04` escalates only a classification whose traffic supports it — so a Tier A hit on a name never reaches the analyst through this input, which `concept/02` itself calls the place 'that bites precisely where it matters most, since the feeds most likely to hit list domains' (433 of the ThreatFox snapshot are domains). Letting TLS SNI satisfy the clause was considered and rejected: it would be a second definition of 'the traffic supports it' under one policy version. (2) THE AGGREGATOR RULE CANNOT BE EXERCISED END TO END. No registered source is an aggregator and no evidence row carries an origin, so `independent_sources` is counted correctly through `helena.enrichment.source_diversity` and demonstrably prevents inflation (forty rows from one source are one vote), but no case in this deployment makes it change an outcome.
makes_buildable: D6 orchestration now has both sides of `concept/03`'s routing `if`, and they are computed from different things: `policy.v1.escalate(policy.supports_in(projection), policy.thresholds())` is the first branch and `triage.escalates(outcome)` is the second. The evidence branch runs whether or not triage produced a result, which is what makes `helena.triage`'s fail-closed safe — `docs/decisions/0021-the-triage-runner.md` §6 recorded that as the one thing the triage stage shipped genuinely unsafe, and it is no longer true. D5 storage gets a second typed record beside the `Decision`: `Escalation` with its `Candidate` rows, `policy_version`, `thresholds_version`, `claims_read` and its gaps — and `claims_read` is what makes 'nothing escalated' and 'there was nothing to read' different rows rather than the same empty one. `config/policy.toml` is the shape any later threshold lands in, and `helena.policy.thresholds()` is the loader that refuses a file a registered Tier B source is missing from.

verification.detail: 1140 passed in 257.93 s, no skips, against the pinned engine (`source bin/env.sh` first) — 46 more than task 32's 1094. 33 of them are new in tests/test_policy.py: 13 table rows (one per escalation rule plus the case each is the negation of), the coverage test over ESCALATION_RULES, the widened gap-kind coverage test over both tables, the two independence tests (a triage `normal` and a triage typed failure beside an escalating Tier A match), the signature-and-AST test that no verdict type is reachable from the evaluator, two aggregator tests, eleven `config/policy.toml` loader tests, and 6 integration tests that build a real context from the committed capture, load the committed ThreatFox extract into a real engine and decide over the view's own `port_matched` and `confidence` rather than over a fixture's idea of them — including a real hit rewritten to confidence 50 so the threshold is decided over a number that travelled the whole mapping view. Five mutations checked, each failed the suite (listed in assumption_validated).

escalations.detail: `thresholds_version` is a tenth version dimension and it is NOT in `helena.versions.VersionSet`. The nine there are what a citable row records; the threshold file is policy that can move without `policy_version` moving, so an escalation that recorded only `policy_version` could not be replayed against the number that decided it. It is recorded on the `Escalation` itself, which is this package's own record and not the agent contract — but if a stored assessment is to carry it beside the other nine, that is a change to `VersionSet` and therefore to the agent contract (`concept/instruction.md` §3). Not blocking: the value is on the record D5 will store anyway. ADR-0023 §4.

No registered source is tier A. `helena.enrichment.SOURCES` holds ThreatFox (B) and sslbl-ja3 (C), so the tier A path — the one `concept/07` names as the failure mode ('triage returning `normal` suppresses a Tier A match') — is exercised by supplying the tier on a `Support` directly rather than by a descriptor. `Support.source_tier` is a plain string and `supports_in` fills it from the registry, so nothing in the store can currently produce a tier A support. Registering one is a governed decision (`concept/05`). Not blocking, and the rule under test is about the tier rather than about the source.

No evidence row carries an `origin`. `concept/02` normalization rule 2 has two halves — count source diversity, and retain the origin an aggregator republished — and the mapping views in `sql/migrations/0014_feed_mapping_views.sql` have no origin column, so `helena.rendering.EntityEnrichment` and therefore `Support` have nowhere to carry one. `_independent_sources` builds `helena.enrichment.Claim` objects with `origin=None`, which is correct for every source registered today and would silently stop being correct the day an aggregator is added. Adding the column is a change to the evidence row's provenance fields. Not blocking; `tests/test_sources.py` exercises the origin half at the `Claim` level. ADR-0023 §5.

deferred: STORING AN ESCALATION. No assessment table exists (task 26 deferred it to D5), so the `Escalation`, its candidates and its gaps are typed and countable in memory and in nothing else — exactly as task 32 left the `Decision`. `concept/instruction.md` §7's 'every new failure path is typed, stored and countable' stays open for the policy layer. What D5 should count here is candidates per rule: a rule that never fires is either wrong or unreachable, and both are worth knowing before the threshold is argued about.

CALLING IT. Nothing invokes `escalate` in a pipeline. `concept/03`'s routing `if` needs a projection, a triage outcome and a trigger to hand the analyst, and assembling those is D6 orchestration's. Wiring it into `helena.triage.run` was rejected for the reason task 32 rejected wiring `constrain` in: the runner is given a bounded rendering and nothing else, and this reads the store.

CALIBRATING THE THRESHOLD. `config/policy.toml`'s 0.80 is a measured position in ThreatFox's own bimodal distribution and NOT a measured escalation rate. `concept/08-open-questions.md` lists the per-source thresholds as blocking and open, and what settles it is labelled outcomes, which do not exist. The file says so and so does ADR-0023 §4.

DOMAIN ESCALATION. Fixing it properly needs the resolution edge — the name to the address the host actually connected to — which the store does not carry. Until it does, a domain hit is capped at `suspicious` by the composition rule and records `domain_scope_untestable`. ADR-0023 §7.

FRESHNESS ADEQUACY. `concept/02` lets tier A establish `malicious` 'if scope and freshness are adequate'; scope is tested and adequate freshness is not. A claim from a superseded snapshot escalates and records the new `freshness_adequacy_untested` gap, because `concept/02` normalization rule 3 says removal from a feed is not exoneration and how much a delisting should reduce confidence is unmeasured.

A CORROBORATION RULE. `independent_sources` is recorded on every candidate and no v1 rule raises anything on it. `concept/04` conditions independent escalation on tier and confidence and on nothing else, and `concept/02`'s 'two independent sources may raise confidence' is written for tier C, which `concept/04` excludes from independent escalation entirely — so a rule lifting a below-threshold tier B claim on corroboration would be inventing a requirement (`concept/instruction.md` §4).
lessons: task 33: THE ESCALATION EVALUATOR BELONGS IN `policy/v1.py` BESIDE `constrain`, NOT IN A MODULE OF ITS OWN. Its third clause — 'whose traffic characteristics support it' — IS the composition rule, so a separate module would have been a second copy of four predicates under one `policy_version`, which is the drift the version rules exist to prevent. What is separate is the INPUT: `supports_in` reads the projection and `supports_for` reads a result's citations, and that difference is the whole of the independence.

task 33: THE INDEPENDENCE INVARIANT IS BROKEN BY AN OPTIMISATION, NOT BY A RULE. Nobody writes a rule that reads the triage verdict on purpose; what happens is a later increment passes the result in so the evaluator can skip work when triage already said `normal`. So the test is over the SIGNATURE and the AST of the three functions the rule reaches, refusing any reference to `AgentResult`, `AgentFailure`, `Decision` or `constrain` — a behavioural test alone would pass for an evaluator that had the result and happened not to read it yet.

task 33: A POLICY FILE NEEDS TWO VERSIONS, AND THE SECOND ONE IS WHY REPLAY STILL WORKS. `policy_version` says which frozen rules the numbers are for (and `escalate` refuses a set written for another, the way `constrain` refuses a result written for another). `thresholds_version` is the file's own and it is recorded on every escalation, because `v1.py` is frozen and `config/policy.toml` is not — a decision that recorded only the module version could not be replayed against the number that actually made it.

task 33: THE LOADER'S COVERAGE CHECK IS THE POINT OF THE LOADER. Refusing a file that is silent about a registered tier B source is what stops a feed escalating on a number nobody chose; refusing a threshold for a tier that reads none is what stops a key nothing applies. Both are `concept/instruction.md` §6's 'silent configuration default' in the two directions it can happen. The out-of-range check earns its place too: `threatfox = 80` — the feed's own 0-100 scale copied in unchanged — would make every claim below threshold and escalate nothing, silently.

task 33: MEASURE THE FEED'S CONFIDENCE DISTRIBUTION BEFORE PICKING A THRESHOLD, BECAUSE IT IS BIMODAL AND THE OBVIOUS VALUE IS DECORATIVE. ThreatFox's `confidence_level` over the committed snapshot: 75 carries 2 254 of 3 375 `ip:port` entries, so a threshold of 0.75 admits 94.3 % of every hit and moves the whole over-alerting risk onto the traffic test. 0.80 is the first value above that mode and admits 27.6 %. Neither number is calibrated; the point is that one of them is not even a filter.

task 33: `Escalation.claims_read` IS WHAT KEEPS `no_match` DISTINCT AT THIS LAYER. A `no_match` carries no evidence identifier, so it contributes no support and is invisible to every rule — which means 'nothing escalated' and 'there was nothing to look at' would otherwise be the same empty record. This is the half of the all-`no_match` problem ADR-0022 §4 said the composition rule could not see, and `tests/test_policy.py::test_a_context_whose_lookups_all_missed_escalates_nothing_and_says_so` is it over a real load.

task 33: A CANDIDATE RECORD FOR EVERY MALICIOUS CLAIM, NOT JUST THE ESCALATING ONES. `concept/07`'s named failure mode — a Tier A match buried — looks exactly like a context with no candidates until somebody can see the candidates and the rule that held each one back. The record answers 'why did this one not escalate', which is the question a quiet stream raises and the one an escalating-only record cannot.
failed_approaches: task 33: Letting a domain observed in TLS SNI or HTTP satisfy `concept/04`'s traffic clause, on the strength of `concept/02`'s 'a name in TLS SNI was connected to, where a name seen only in a DNS query may never have been'. Rejected before it was written: `helena.policy.v1._name_carries_no_traffic` already caps domain-only support at `suspicious` for the context verdict, so this would have been a second, disagreeing definition of 'the traffic supports it' inside one `policy_version` — the same claim escalating as malicious while the composition rule refused to let a verdict say so. The under-firing is recorded as a passing test and an ADR section instead.

task 33: Making corroboration for the shared-infrastructure case require an INDEPENDENT SOURCE at escalation time, so the aggregator rule would visibly change an outcome. Rejected: `helena.policy.v1._shared_infrastructure` defines corroboration as a supporting claim that is not itself on shared infrastructure, and redefining it here would put two meanings of one word in one frozen version. With one address-claiming feed registered it would also have made every resolver hit unescalatable for a reason that is about the registry rather than about the evidence.

task 33: Adding an `origin` field to `helena.policy.Support` so `source_diversity`'s aggregator half could be exercised end to end. Nothing in the store produces an origin — there is no such column in `sql/migrations/0014_feed_mapping_views.sql` — so the field would have had exactly one value in every code path, which is the speculative abstraction `concept/instruction.md` §1 refuses. Escalated as a provenance question instead.

task 33: Treating a `stale` claim as one that does not escalate, on the strength of tier A's 'if scope and freshness are adequate'. Rejected against `concept/02` normalization rule 3: 'removal from a feed is not exoneration', and delisting MAY reduce confidence — by an amount nobody has measured. Suppressing on staleness would have been inventing exactly the threshold the gap now records as missing.

task 33: Building the escalation input by reusing `supports_for` with a synthesised result citing every claim. It would have worked and it would have put an `AgentResult` in the escalation path, which is the one thing the invariant forbids; `supports_in` is six lines and has nowhere for a verdict to enter.
next_session_should_know: Both halves of `concept/03`'s routing `if` now exist and neither reads the other. FIVE THINGS TO CARRY. (1) THE CALL IS THREE LINES AND NONE OF THEM MENTIONS TRIAGE: `supports = policy.supports_in(projection)`, `limits = policy.thresholds()`, `policy.version('v1').escalate(supports, limits)`. `PolicyVersion` now carries both `constrain` and `escalate`, so a stored `policy_version` gives you the whole rule set. `escalate` raises `PolicyError` only for a threshold set written for another policy version, and for a tier B source with no configured threshold; disagreement with anything is the return value. (2) THE ORDER OF THE ROUTING `if` MATTERS AND IS `concept/03`'s: the evidence branch is FIRST and its trigger is `deterministic_signal`, the triage branch second with `triage_suspicious`. `helena.contracts.v1` already closes the trigger vocabulary over the three; check it rather than inventing a fourth. (3) `escalate` RUNS FOR A CONTEXT WHOSE TRIAGE FAILED, AND THAT IS THE POINT. `helena.triage.escalates` still returns `False` for every typed failure, and the pipeline is now safe to fail closed because this reads the store instead. Anything that skips the evaluator when triage failed re-opens exactly the hole ADR-0021 §6 recorded. (4) TWO RECORDS TO STORE, NOT ONE. D5 needs `Decision` (task 32) and `Escalation` (this one) beside the assessment; they answer different questions and neither is derivable from the other. `Escalation` carries `thresholds_version`, which is NOT one of `VersionSet`'s nine — see the escalation in this report before deciding where it lands. (5) `config/policy.toml`'s 0.80 IS A CANDIDATE AND THE FILE SAYS SO. Do not cite it as a calibrated threshold anywhere; `concept/08` still lists per-source thresholds as blocking and open, and the only thing that closes it is a labelled corpus. The full suite is now 1 140 tests in ~258 s on this machine, with no skips.
